content: The review question investigates the impact of workplace ventilation, personal protective equipment (PPE), and organizational strategies on reducing exposure to manufactured nanomaterials (MNMs) in occupational settings. The effectiveness of these controls is measured using the protection factor (PF), which is the ratio of exposure levels without controls to those with controls. A PF greater than 1 indicates a reduction in exposure, with a PF of 10 signifying a 90% reduction. A systematic review by Myojo and Nagata (2017) included 50 studies across 55 workplaces. Of these, 27 studies used before-and-after comparisons. Ventilation was evaluated in 14 studies involving 27 workplaces, PPE in 19 studies with 23 participants, and other control strategies in 16 studies. These strategies included fluid-based dust suppression, process automation, organizational measures, and the use of safety data sheets (SDS). All studies focused on MNM exposure, with 15 specifically addressing carbon nanotubes. Outcomes were expressed as PF values. The main limitations of the studies were the absence of control groups for engineering controls and the lack of fieldwork for respiratory protection studies. The risk of bias was rated between 2 and 3 on a scale from -3 (very high risk) to +3 (very low risk). For engineering controls, enclosures achieved the highest PFs (>100 in seven cases), while ventilation effectiveness depended on factors such as air velocity and worker movements. Respiratory protection, such as N95 respirators, provided PFs greater than 10 in 11 cases, while P100 respirators achieved PFs around 100. Most studies were conducted under ideal laboratory conditions, often using sodium chloride as a proxy for MNMs, raising concerns about the applicability of these findings to real-world workplaces. The quality of evidence was generally low due to non-randomized and non-controlled study designs. The evidence was consistent across studies but lacked statistical precision. Publication bias was expected but could not be assessed due to insufficient data. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) concluded that there is low-quality evidence supporting the effectiveness of engineering controls, such as enclosures and ventilation, in reducing MNM exposure. Similarly, there is low-quality evidence that respiratory protection can significantly reduce exposure if the appropriate type is used and fit-testing is conducted. The GDG recommends further field studies to evaluate dust control techniques and the effectiveness of respiratory protection in real workplace conditions. Regarding control-banding tools for MNM exposure, a systematic review by Eastlake, Zumwalde, and Geraci (2016) evaluated two studies involving 32 exposure scenarios. The control-banding nanotool's recommendations aligned with those of occupational hygienists in 59% of cases, recommended lower controls in 28%, and higher controls in 13%. However, no exposure assessment data were provided to verify the effectiveness of the recommended controls. The evidence was downgraded to very low quality due to study limitations, including qualitative analysis and lack of exposure measurements. The GDG concluded that there is very low-quality evidence that the control-banding nanotool provides similar recommendations to those of experienced occupational hygienists. Training for professionals, employers, and workers is necessary to use the tool effectively. Further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of control-banding tools in reducing MNM exposure and to calibrate these tools against exposure measurements. Health surveillance for workers exposed to MNMs was also reviewed. A systematic review by Gulumian et al. (2016) included seven studies, six of which compared health indicators between exposed and unexposed workers. Biomarkers of oxidative stress and early health effects, such as pulmonary and neurobehavioral test results, were reported. However, no controlled longitudinal studies were available, and the evidence was downgraded to very low quality due to study design limitations. The GDG found very low-quality evidence on whether targeted health surveillance for MNMs could detect early signs of adverse health effects. More research is needed to identify specific biomarkers, validate medical tests, and assess the long-term health effects of MNM exposure. Workers participating in health surveillance should be informed that these programs are research efforts with unproven benefits. Training and worker involvement in health and safety practices are considered best practices, but no studies were found to evaluate the effects of specific training or worker participation on MNM exposure or control implementation. The GDG recommends research to assess the impact of training and worker involvement on exposure levels and control measures. The implementation of these guidelines requires significant efforts from all stakeholders, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. WHO plans to launch the guidelines with its partners and prepare simplified summaries for employers and workers to facilitate implementation and monitoring.
